title: Equivalence I(epsilon, nu) is I(epsilon, -nu)
statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$, $

If $

u$, this is the usual normalization $A(

u)$.

At an exceptional parameter $
u\in\mathcal W_\varepsilon$, $

u|$. The unnormalized $A(

u=-n$ it kills the finite-dimensional submodule with $|r|\le n-1$. Moreover, $I_{\varepsilon,n}$ and $I_{\varepsilon,-n}$ are not isomorphic as $(\mathfrak g,K)$-modules, and therefore are not continuously equivalent as smooth $G$-representations: the former has irreducible tail submodules, whereas the latter has the finite-dimensional submodule as its unique irreducible submodule, and their $K$-type supports are disjoint. At $\varepsilon=1,
u=0$, the two representations coincide and the odd K-finite module splits into the two limit chains by [[thm-generic-irreducibility-and-the-exceptional-parameter-lattice]](b). Thus $I_{\varepsilon,

strategy: Normalize the meromorphic K-type family by its parity base scalar. Extend the quotient across the common poles, use the cross-parameter recurrence for a two-sided inverse, and prove the G-intertwining identity by continuity. On the imaginary axis the normalized multipliers have modulus one. At nonzero exceptional parameters compare a locally proved simple tail submodule with the unique finite-dimensional irreducible submodule on the opposite side.
